newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-AWB boosts Australia wheat to record 23 MT.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-AWB boosts Australia wheat to record 23 MT.

text.p: The Australian Wheat Board (AWB) said it further upgraded the Australian wheat crop to a record 23 million tonnes.
Earlier on Monday, the AWB said in a weekly market report dated Friday that it had raised its 1996/97 estimate to 22 million tonnes from 21.5 million.
This was one million tonnes bigger than Australia's previous record crop, in 1983/84, it said.
"Australia has just harvested a 23 million tonne wheat crop," AWB general manager merchandising Ron Storey said, while announcing a A$3.00 a tonne price increase for most Australian wheat grades.
The amount of on-farm storage now in use made it difficult to be precise about the crop size but the tonnage already received by the AWB pointed to a 23 million tonne crop, he said.
Storey also said Australia had had an outstanding start to its selling season.
"Last week we announced a 1.5 million tonne sale to Iran, one of our oldest customers.

"That's been the largest single sale we've concluded so far this year but a combination of sales to old customers, new customers and some opportunistic sales sees us in the position of having half our potential exports now priced.
"This is a year for breaking records. We've settled down to market the biggest crop on record with an unprecedented first quarter shipping programme," he said.
Australia would ship record tonnages in January, February and March, he said.
The AWB estimated it would export close to 17 million tonnes of wheat in the current year, almost half as much again as a normal crop, he said.
There was still a considerable amount of wheat to be sold in the second part of the current year.
This made it very difficult to accurately estimate the final return for the pool, Storey said.

"We're really in unknown territory," he said. "We know that we'll be competing with U.S. and European supplies but we still don't have a clear idea of how much we will have to compete with or what sort of demand pattern will emerge."
AWB was still seeing buyers take a conservative approach, pricing wheat no more than two months ahead, he said. This indicated they expected plentiful supplies to continue.
The fundamentals of world wheat supply had not changed greatly, remaining historically tight, he said.
Any partial crop failure would affect the market.
"We have a long year ahead of us but we've made a great start," he said.
The next pool return revision will be on February 3.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
